dublinCore.description: Interactive MicroSim showing five classic continuous-time Fourier transform pairs (rectangle and sinc, Gaussian and Gaussian, one-sided exponential and Lorentzian magnitude, cosine and two impulses, impulse train and impulse train). The analytic transform is overlaid on a 16384-point FFT estimate of the sampled signal, a time-scale slider shows that compressing in time expands in frequency, and a time-shift slider shows the resulting linear phase ramp.

learningObjectives: Identify the transform of a rectangular pulse, a Gaussian, a one-sided exponential, a cosine and an impulse train
Predict how the height and width of |X(f)| change when a signal is compressed or stretched in time, using x(t/T) <-> T X(fT)
Calculate the phase that a time shift adds at a given frequency, using x(t - t0) <-> e^(-j 2 pi f t0) X(f)
Explain why the Gaussian reaches the smallest time-bandwidth product, sigma_t sigma_f = 1/(4 pi)
Read a transform pair backwards, identifying x(t) from a given X(f) (the inverse Fourier transform)

misconceptions.misconception: Delaying a signal changes its spectrum
misconceptions.correction: A delay multiplies X(f) by e^(-j 2 pi f t0): the magnitude is unchanged and only the phase gains a linear ramp
misconceptions.evidence: Drag the shift slider: the green magnitude dots do not move while the phase plot tilts into a ramp of -360 t0 degrees per hertz

misconceptions.misconception: A narrower pulse has a narrower spectrum
misconceptions.correction: x(t/T) <-> T X(fT): compressing in time expands the spectrum and lowers its peak
misconceptions.evidence: For the rectangle, lowering T from 1 s to 0.5 s moves the first zero from 1 Hz to 2 Hz and lowers X(0) from 1 to 0.5

accessibility.screenReaderScript: Three stacked plots for a chosen Fourier transform pair: the time signal x(t) in blue, the magnitude |X(f)| and the phase of X(f). Analytic curves are maroon and green dots are the FFT of the sampled signal. Gold bars mark the width in time and in frequency. A drop-down picks the pair, a slider sets the time scale T, a slider sets the time shift t0, and a checkbox shows or hides the phase plot.

controls.label: Transform pair
controls.description: Chooses the Fourier transform pair shown in the three plots

controls.label: Show phase
controls.description: Shows the phase plot; when it is hidden the magnitude plot uses the extra height

controls.label: Time scale T
controls.description: Replaces x(t) with x(t/T), which transforms to T X(fT): pulse width, Gaussian width, exponential time constant 1/a, cosine period or impulse spacing

controls.label: Shift t0
controls.description: Delays the signal by t0 seconds, which multiplies X(f) by e^(-j 2 pi f t0); the impulse train's shift is rounded to its sample grid of T/256

visualElements.description: Time plot: x(t) in blue (impulses as arrows of area 1) with a gold bar marking its width
Magnitude plot: analytic |X(f)| in maroon (impulse areas as arrows), FFT estimate as green dots, and a gold bar marking the spectral width
Phase plot: analytic phase of X(f) in maroon and FFT phase as green dots, drawn where |X| exceeds 2% of X(0)
Read-outs: the transform pair formula, the widths in time and frequency with FFT-measured values, the phase added by the shift, and the largest FFT error

model.description: Evaluates the analytic transform of x(t/T) delayed by t0 and compares it with a numerical estimate: x(t) is sampled (cell averages where it jumps) every 1/128 s over a 128 s window, or every T/256 s over 64 whole periods for the periodic pairs, transformed with a 16384-point radix-2 FFT and scaled by the sample spacing (and by the bin width for impulse areas)
equations: X(f) = integral x(t) e^(-j 2 pi f t) dt
x(t) = integral X(f) e^(j 2 pi f t) df
exp(-pi t^2 / T^2) <-> T exp(-pi f^2 T^2)
sum_n delta(t - nT) <-> (1/T) sum_k delta(f - k/T)
x(t - t0) <-> e^(-j 2 pi f t0) X(f)
algorithms: V-fit refinement of the first sinc zero
Linear interpolation of the half-power frequency
limitations: The FFT estimate covers |f| < 64 Hz (aperiodic pairs), so tiny aliasing and cell-averaging errors remain (largest about 0.06% of X(0))
The impulse train's shift is rounded to the nearest multiple of T/256 (at most 0.004 s)

instructionalStrategies: Predict the effect of halving T before moving the slider
Compare the analytic curve with the FFT dots to trust both
Read pairs backwards to practise the inverse transform
extensions: Add the duality pair sinc <-> rectangle
Add modulation (frequency shift) by multiplying x(t) by a cosine
